planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Baldwin is a University of Florida-bred fig selected for good resistance to fruit souring in humid, rainy climates where many other fig varieties spoil on the tree.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; figs tolerate poor soils better than most fruit trees and do well in raised beds or large containers where restricted roots encourage fruiting over rampant growth. Baldwin was developed at a University of Florida research station and selected specifically for resistance to souring, a common problem in the Gulf South and Florida where warm, humid weather during ripening lets yeasts and bacteria enter the open eye of the fruit and spoil it before harvest. The medium, brown-skinned fruit has sweet, pink-amber flesh and a closed eye that helps keep out rain and insects, giving Baldwin an edge over open-eyed varieties in humid climates. It produces a reliable main crop in late summer without needing a pollinator, and benefits from a thick mulch layer and occasional deep watering during dry spells.

common_name: Maiden Blush Apple (Early American Heirloom Dual-Purpose Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Maiden Blush is a New Jersey heirloom dating to the late 1700s, grown for its pale, translucent yellow skin blushed with red and its dual use fresh and in cooking.

directions: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, and provide a compatible pollinator, since Maiden Blush is not reliably self-fruitful. First noted in New Jersey in the late eighteenth century, Maiden Blush became one of the most widely planted American heirloom apples of the nineteenth century for its striking pale lemon-yellow skin marked with a rosy pink blush on the sun-exposed side, a color pattern early writers likened to a blushing cheek. The crisp, tart-leaning flesh cooks down into a pale, delicately flavored sauce and dries well, while a fully ripe apple mellows enough for pleasant fresh eating, making it a genuinely dual-purpose variety by the standards of its era. It ripens over a fairly early late-summer window and does not keep as long in storage as later-season heirlooms, so plan to use or process the crop within a few weeks of picking. Thin heavy fruit set in early summer to improve size and reduce biennial bearing.

common_name: Anise Basil (Licorice Basil, Thai Anise Basil)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant out once soil has warmed, or direct sow after frost danger has passed; Anise Basil is an old heirloom basil type with purple-tinged stems and flower spikes and a pronounced anise-licorice flavor distinct from sweet basil.

directions: Transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade after all frost danger has passed, since basil is quickly killed by cold. Anise Basil, sometimes called licorice basil, is a classic heirloom type with dark purple stems, purple-flushed leaf veins, and tall spikes of pinkish-purple flowers that make it as ornamental as it is useful in the kitchen, where its bold anise-licorice flavor is prized in Vietnamese and Persian cooking and pairs well with fruit, fish, and Asian-style dishes that sweet basil can't match. Pinch growing tips regularly and remove flower spikes as they form to keep the plant bushy and productive through the season, though leaving a few spikes to bloom brings in a steady stream of pollinators. It tolerates the heat and humidity of a Gulf Coast summer as well as most basils and will grow in a large container with the same care as sweet basil.

common_name: Dragon Tails Hosta (Twisted Narrow-Leaf Gold-Centered Hosta)

planting.note: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Dragon Tails is a narrow, twisted-leaf novelty hosta in the same distinctive group as Praying Hands, forming a dense, upright, spiky-looking clump unlike a typical broad-leaved hosta.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, giving a little morning sun where summers are mild to keep the gold leaf centers bright. Dragon Tails belongs to the small, distinctive group of hosta novelties with narrow, twisted, upright leaves that stay folded along their length rather than lying flat, giving the clump a spiky, almost grass-like texture that stands out sharply next to broad-leaved hostas nearby. Each leaf shows a chartreuse-to-gold center against a dark green margin, and the unusual habit makes it an excellent textural accent in a shaded border or container rather than a mass groundcover plant. Pale lavender flowers rise on scapes above the foliage in summer. Divide congested clumps in spring every three to four years, and watch for slugs, which target the tender new growth as it emerges.

common_name: Fried Green Tomatoes Hosta (Large Corrugated Green Hosta)

planting.note: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Fried Green Tomatoes is a large, vigorous hosta with glossy, deeply corrugated green leaves related to the popular Sum and Substance breeding line.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, and give the clump plenty of room, since this is a large, spreading hosta that needs several seasons to reach full size. Fried Green Tomatoes produces broad, rounded, glossy medium-green leaves with heavy corrugation and slightly rippled margins, forming a substantial mounding clump that works well as a bold specimen or anchor plant in a shaded border. Pale lavender-white flowers appear on tall scapes in mid to late summer, though the leaves are the main attraction. Like other large-leaved hostas it tolerates a bit more sun than thin-leaved cultivars if the soil stays consistently moist, but performs best out of hot afternoon exposure in Southern gardens. Divide only when necessary, since large hostas resent frequent disturbance and take a season or two to recover their full size afterward.
